      <content name="title"><span class="qt1">Ulcerative</span> <span class="qt0">Colitis</span></content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle"><span class="qt0">Colitis</span></content>

      <content name="altTitle"><span class="qt1">Ulcerative</span> proctitis</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p><span class="qt1">Ulcerative</span> <span class="qt0">colitis</span> (UC) is a disease that causes inflammation and sores, called <span class="qt2">ulcers</span>, in the lining of the rectum and colon. It is one of a group of diseases called inflammatory bowel disease.</p><p>UC can happen at any age, but it usually starts between the ages of 15 and 30. It tends to run in families. The most common symptoms are pain in the abdomen and blood or pus in diarrhea. Other symptoms may include:</p><ul><li>Anemia</li><li>Severe tiredness</li><li>Weight loss</li><li>Loss of appetite</li><li>Bleeding from the rectum</li><li>Sores on the skin</li><li>Joint pain</li><li>Growth failure in children</li></ul><p>About half of people with UC have mild symptoms.</p><p>Doctors use blood tests, stool tests, colonoscopy or sigmoidoscopy, and imaging tests to diagnose UC. Several types of drugs can help control it. Some people have long periods of remission, when they are free of symptoms. In severe cases, doctors must remove the colon.</p><p>NIH: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases</p></content>

    <document rank="1" url="https://medlineplus.gov/colonicdiseases.html">
      <content name="title">Colonic Diseases</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Intestinal Diseases</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Large intestine diseases</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>Your colon, also known as the large intestine, is part of your digestive system. It's a long, hollow tube at the end of your digestive tract where your body makes and stores stool. Many disorders affect the colon's ability to work properly. Some of these include:</p><ul><li>Colorectal cancer</li><li>Colonic polyps - extra tissue growing in the colon that can become cancerous</li><li><span class="qt1">Ulcerative</span> <span class="qt0">colitis</span> - <span class="qt2">ulcers</span> of the colon and rectum</li><li>Diverticulitis - inflammation or infection of pouches in the colon</li><li>Irritable bowel syndrome  -  an uncomfortable condition causing abdominal cramping and other symptoms</li></ul><p>Treatment for colonic diseases varies greatly depending on the disease and its severity. Treatment may involve diet, medicines and in some cases, surgery.</p><p>NIH: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases</p></content>

    <document rank="2" url="https://medlineplus.gov/crohnsdisease.html">
      <content name="title">Crohn's Disease</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Ileocolitis</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Inflammatory Bowel Disease</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Regional Enteritis</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Regional Ileitis</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is Crohn's disease?<p>Crohn's disease is a chronic (long-lasting) disease that causes inflammation in your digestive tract. It can affect any part of your digestive tract, which runs from your mouth to your anus. But it usually affects your small intestine and the beginning of your large intestine.</p><p>Crohn's disease is an inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). <span class="qt1">Ulcerative</span> <span class="qt0">colitis</span> and microscopic <span class="qt0">colitis</span> are other common types of IBD.</p>What causes Crohn's disease?<p>The cause of Crohn's disease is unknown. Researchers think that an autoimmune reaction may be one cause. An autoimmune reaction happens when your immune system attacks healthy cells in your body. Genetics may also play a role, since Crohn's disease can run in families.</p><p>Stress and eating certain foods don't cause the disease, but they can make your symptoms worse.</p>Who is more likely to develop Crohn's disease?<p>There are certain factors that may raise your risk of Crohn's disease:</p><ul><li>Family history of the disease. Having a parent, child, or sibling with the disease puts you at higher risk.</li><li>Smoking. This may double your risk of developing Crohn's disease.</li><li>Certain medicines, such as antibiotics, birth-control pills, and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) such as aspirin or ibuprofen. These may slightly increase your chance of developing Crohn's.</li><li>A high-fat diet. This may also slightly increase your risk of Crohn's.</li></ul>What are the symptoms of Crohn's disease?<p>The symptoms of Crohn's disease can vary, depending where and how severe your inflammation is. The most common symptoms include:</p><ul><li>Diarrhea</li><li>Cramping and pain in your abdomen</li><li>Weight loss</li></ul><p>Some other possible symptoms are:</p><ul><li>Anemia, a condition in which you have fewer red blood cells than normal</li><li>Eye redness or pain</li><li>Fatigue</li><li>Fever</li><li>Joint pain or soreness</li><li>Nausea or loss of appetite</li><li>Skin changes that involve red, tender bumps under the skin</li></ul><p>Stress and eating certain foods such as carbonated (fizzy) drinks and high-fiber foods may make some people's symptoms worse.</p>What other problems can Crohn's disease cause?<p>Crohn's disease can cause other problems, including:</p><ul><li>Intestinal obstruction, a blockage in the intestine</li><li>Fistulas, abnormal connections between two parts inside of the body</li><li>Abscesses, pus-filled pockets of infection</li><li>Anal fissures, small tears in your anus that may cause itching, pain, or bleeding</li><li><span class="qt2">Ulcers</span>, open sores in your mouth, intestines, anus, or perineum</li><li>Malnutrition, when your body does not get the right amount of vitamins, minerals, and nutrients it needs</li><li>Inflammation in other areas of your body, such as your joints, eyes, and skin</li></ul>How is Crohn's disease diagnosed?<p>Your health care provider may use many tools to make a diagnosis:</p><ul><li>A medical history, which includes asking about your symptoms</li><li>A family history</li><li>A physical exam, including:
	<ul><li>Checking for bloating in your abdomen.</li><li>Listening to sounds within your abdomen using a stethoscope.</li><li>Tapping on your abdomen to check for tenderness and pain and to see if your liver or spleen is abnormal or enlarged.</li></ul>
</li><li>Various tests, including:
	<ul><li>Blood and stool tests.</li><li>A colonoscopy.</li><li>An upper GI endoscopy, a procedure in which your provider uses a scope to look inside your mouth, esophagus, stomach, and small intestine.</li><li>Diagnostic imaging tests, such as a CT scan or an upper GI series. An upper GI series uses a special liquid called barium and x-rays. Drinking the barium will make your upper GI tract more visible on an x-ray.</li></ul>
</li></ul>What are the treatments for Crohn's disease?<p>There is no cure for Crohn's disease, but treatments can decrease inflammation in your intestines, relieve symptoms, and prevent complications. Treatments include medicines, bowel rest, and surgery. No single treatment works for everyone. You and your provider can work together to figure out which treatment is best for you:</p><ul><li>Medicines for Crohn's include various medicines that decrease the inflammation. Many of these medicines do this by reducing the activity of your immune system. Certain medicines can also help with symptoms or complications, such as nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and anti-diarrheal medicines. If your Crohn's causes an infection, you may need antibiotics.</li><li>Bowel rest involves drinking only certain liquids or not eating or drinking anything. This allows your intestines to rest. You may need to do this if your Crohn's disease symptoms are severe. You get your nutrients through drinking a liquid, a feeding tube, or an intravenous (IV) tube. You may need to do bowel rest in the hospital, or you may be able to do it at home. It will last for a few days or up to several weeks.</li><li>Surgery can treat complications and reduce symptoms when other treatments are not helping enough. The surgery will involve removing a damaged part of your digestive tract to treat:
	<ul><li>Fistulas</li><li>Bleeding that is life threatening</li><li>Intestinal obstructions</li><li>Side effects from medicines when they threaten your health</li><li>Symptoms when medicines do not improve your condition</li></ul>
</li></ul><p>Changing your diet can help reduce symptoms. Your provider may recommend that you make changes to your diet, such as:</p><ul><li>Avoiding carbonated drinks</li><li>Avoiding popcorn, vegetable skins, nuts, and other high-fiber foods</li><li>Drinking more liquids</li><li>Eating smaller meals more often</li><li>Keeping a food diary to help identify foods that cause problems</li></ul><p>In some cases, your provider may ask you to go on a special diet, such as a diet that is:</p><ul><li>High calorie</li><li>Lactose free</li><li>Low fat</li><li>Low fiber</li><li>Low salt</li></ul><p>If you are not absorbing enough nutrients, you may need to take nutritional supplements and vitamins.</p><p>NIH: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases</p></content>

    <document rank="3" url="https://medlineplus.gov/ankylosingspondylitis.html">
      <content name="title">Ankylosing Spondylitis</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Rheumatoid Spondylitis</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Spondylitis, Ankylosing</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is ankylosing spondylitis?<p>Ankylosing spondylitis (AS) is a type of arthritis of the spine. It causes inflammation (swelling) between your vertebrae (the bones that make up your spine) and the joints between your spine and pelvis. AS inflammation can cause stiffness and make it difficult to move and bend.</p><p>Symptoms of AS can range from mild to severe back pain. Over time, AS can fuse (grow together) your vertebrae, limiting movement and causing a hunched posture. In some people, AS can affect other joints or body parts.</p><p>There is no cure for AS, but early treatment can help manage symptoms, slow down the disease, and help you lead a more productive life.</p>Who is more likely to get ankylosing spondylitis?<p>Ankylosing spondylitis usually starts before age 45. Early symptoms may begin between the ages of 15 and 30. Your chance of developing AS can also increase if:</p><ul><li>You're a man. AS is more common and severe in men.</li><li>You have a family history. If a member of your family has AS, you're more likely to get the disease.</li><li>You have other medical conditions that may increase your risk of getting AS. These include Crohn's disease, <span class="qt1">ulcerative</span> <span class="qt0">colitis</span>, or psoriasis.</li></ul>What causes ankylosing spondylitis?<p>No one knows what causes ankylosing spondylitis, but the environment and genes likely play a role. Your genes are parts of DNA in your cells that are passed down from your parents. Certain genes may increase your risk of getting the disease, but not everyone with these genes gets AS.</p>What are the symptoms of ankylosing spondylitis?<p>AS affects people differently. The most common symptom is pain and stiffness in the lower back and/or hips. The pain is usually worse during the night or after sitting for a long time.</p><p>Over time, AS may progress to other areas of your spine or body. Symptoms may depend on which areas of your body the disease affects. Some people have symptoms that come and go. Others may have severe, ongoing pain.</p><p>Other symptoms of ankylosing spondylitis may include:</p><ul><li>Pain, stiffness, and inflammation of the joints.</li><li>Difficulty taking a deep breath. This could occur if the joints connecting the ribs are affected.</li><li>Changes in vision.</li><li>Fatigue.</li><li>Loss of appetite.</li><li>Weight loss.</li><li>Skin rashes, such as psoriasis.</li><li>Abdominal (belly) pain and loose stools (poop).</li></ul>How is ankylosing spondylitis diagnosed?<p>There is no single test for ankylosing spondylitis. To find out if you have AS your health care provider may:</p><ul><li>Ask about your medical history, including your symptoms.</li><li>Ask about your family health history, including relatives who have had AS.</li><li>Do a physical exam.</li><li>Order blood tests or imaging studies.</li></ul>What are the treatments for ankylosing spondylitis?<p>AS has no cure, but treatment may help relieve symptoms, maintain posture, and slow down the disease. Since other parts of your body can be affected by AS, you will likely work with a team of health care professionals for tests, diagnosis, and care.</p><p>Treatment usually includes medicine to help relieve symptoms and keep the disease from getting worse, as well as physical therapy to improve mobility. If AS is severe, surgery may be needed.</p><p>You can help manage your AS symptoms if you:</p><ul><li>Exercise</li><li>Monitor your symptoms</li><li>Manage your stress</li><li>Use assistive devices as needed</li><li>Follow a healthy diet</li><li>Stop smoking, or don't start</li></ul><p>NIH: National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Disease</p></content>

    <document rank="4" url="https://medlineplus.gov/bileductcancer.html">
      <content name="title">Bile Duct Cancer</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Cholangiocarcinoma</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>Your liver makes a digestive juice called bile. Your gallbladder stores it between meals. When you eat, your gallbladder pushes the bile into tubes called bile ducts. They carry the bile to your small intestine. The bile helps break down fat. It also helps the liver get rid of toxins and wastes.</p><p>Bile duct cancer is rare. It can happen in the parts of the bile ducts that are outside or inside the liver. Cancer of the bile duct outside of the liver is much more common. Risk factors include having inflammation of the bile duct, <span class="qt1">ulcerative</span> <span class="qt0">colitis</span>, and some liver diseases.</p><p>Symptoms can include:</p><ul><li>Jaundice</li><li>Itchy skin</li><li>Fever</li><li>Abdominal pain</li></ul><p>Tests to diagnose bile duct cancer may include a physical exam, imaging tests of the liver and bile ducts, blood tests, and a biopsy.</p><p>Treatments include surgery, radiation therapy, and chemotherapy.</p><p>NIH: National Cancer Institute</p></content>
